title: TikTok and adolescent vision health: Content and information quality assessment of the top short videos related to myopia
screen_reason: Content analysis of the 168 eligible videos among the top 200 most-liked myopia videos on the Chinese version of TikTok (searched 12 March 2022). Two clinician raters coded video content against International Myopia Institute 2019/2021 guideline reports and report a 'crude prevalence' of misinformation of 10.1% (17/168). That is a quantitative share of items judged against an external ground truth with a stated denominator. The paper's DISCERN and PEMAT-A/V outputs are QUALITY instruments but are reported only as means, so they generate no rows.

estimates.country: China (Chinese version of the TikTok app, search term '近视' [myopia])
estimates.date: Search and screening on March 12, 2022; videos had been posted for a median of 230 days (IQR 164-307)
estimates.measure_type: % of top-liked myopia videos on Chinese TikTok containing misinformation (statements not accurate or sufficiently rigorous against International Myopia Institute guidance)
estimates.value_raw: 10.1% (17/168); 19 descriptions determined as misinformation in 17 videos
estimates.denominator: 168 myopia-related TikTok videos: the top 200 most-liked of 423 retrieved by the keyword '近视' (myopia), after removing unrelated and duplicated videos and those with no audio or text
estimates.definition: A video description was counted as misinformation if it was 'not accurate or sufficiently rigorous' when compared with the International Myopia Institute standards (2021 yearly digest as the main reference; the 2019 IMI definition report and 2021 risk-factors guideline for diagnostic and risk content; the 2019 IMI white paper on clinical management for management content). Examples in Table 2 include 'Myopia can cause hearing loss', 'Myopia is recoverable' and 'Sweet food or sodas cause myopia'.
estimates.misinfo_def: The paper gives no formal definition of misinformation; operationally, 'Content was evaluated using a predefined scoring system based on works published by the International Myopia Institute in 2019 or 2021, which were also the standards for characterizing misleading information.'
estimates.source_quote: A total of 19 descriptions were determined as misinformation in 17 videos. The total crude prevalence was 10.1% (17/168)
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Prevalence of misinformation', p. 04; Table 3 (Misinformation, n (%): 17 (10.1)); Table 2 lists the 19 flagged descriptions
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 'The evaluations were performed by one ophthalmologist and one eye public health physician independently (XK and MS), based on the official handbooks.' Raters saw only the videos; uploader information and classification were concealed to avoid selection bias. Discrepancies resolved by discussion. Reliability reported for the DISCERN total score (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.957, 95% CI 0.931-0.972, P < 0.001) and for source classification (93.5% agreement, kappa 0.906, P < 0.001); NO reliability statistic is reported for the misinformation coding itself. External benchmark: International Myopia Institute 2019 and 2021 reports.
estimates.moderator_quote: the 'most likes' ranking algorithm was chosen to sort the retrieved 423 videos. Among these, videos ranked beyond 200 were less likely to be originated by the publisher and less likely to be viewed by users. Thus, only the top 200 most-liked videos were included for further eligibility evaluation.
estimates.notes: Single-issue (myopia) keyword corpus that is also rank-truncated to the top 200 most-liked, hence denom_scope=topical with denom_selection=curated. Coded CONTENT, not QUALITY, because this specific number comes from a claim-level accuracy judgement against named clinical guidelines and is reported by the authors as 'prevalence of misinformation' - distinct from the paper's DISCERN/PEMAT quality scoring. FLAG FOR ADJUDICATOR: the Table 2 header is 'Descriptions that were not accurate or sufficiently rigorous', and several flagged items are over-absolute rather than plainly false ('Too absolute: no eyedrops (without excluding atropine) are helpful for myopia'), so breadth is coded 'misleading' rather than 'false'. Topic is health_other (myopia / adolescent vision health), not covid19.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) Source-type splits of the misinformation prevalence are verbatim in Table 3 but were not written as rows because they are actor-type subgroups within one country x platform cell, not country/platform/measure splits, and several cells are tiny: non-profit organizations 1/32 (3.1%), for-profit organizations 3/15 (20.0%), news agencies 0/12 (0%), individual non-medical users 10/32 (31.3%), medical individual users 3/77 (3.9%). 2) No QUALITY rows were written even though the study uses DISCERN and PEMAT-A/V, because every quality output is a mean or a mean percentage score across videos rather than a share of videos: DISCERN total 38.2/80 (SD 7.6), publication reliability 19.8 (2.5 per item), treatment-choice 17.2 (2.5 per item, n = 107), overall quality item-16 score 3.1 (0.9), PEMAT-A/V understandability 84.7% (11.7%), actionability 74.9% (38.0%). The instructions treat a scale reported only as a mean as not a share. An adjudicator who wants a QUALITY row could instead use the trichotomised DISCERN overall-quality distribution in Table 3 (Low 27/107 = 25.2%, Moderate 41 = 38.3%, High 39 = 36.4%), which IS a share of videos - not extracted because the thresholds for Low/Moderate/High are never defined in the text. 3) Content-coverage shares (management partly or fully addressed 137/168 = 81.5%; outcomes 138/168 = 82.1%; 'definition' not even addressed 129/168 = 76.8%; 3-4 content areas 92/168 = 54.8%; 5-6 areas 21/168 = 12.5%) are completeness measures, not veracity, so no rows. 4) Engagement totals (2,246,062 likes, 101,582 comments, 352,365 shares) are never expressed as a share going to misinformation, so no EXPOSURE or SHARING row is derivable. 5) Prevalence figures for other TikTok topics quoted in the Discussion (genitourinary cancers 36.1%, prostate cancer 41.2%, ADHD 52%, mask use 10.6%, pediatric urological disease 77.8%) are cited from other papers - excluded under R8. 6) Minor internal inconsistency for the record: the abstract prints 'definition (86.9%, 146/169)' where the denominator elsewhere is 168.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content and quality analysis of a rank-truncated TikTok search set. Frame: a single keyword search ('近视', myopia) in the Chinese TikTok app on 12 March 2022 sorted by 'most likes', returning 423 videos; only the top 200 most-liked were screened, and after removing unrelated, duplicated and audio/text-free videos, 168 were analysed. No probability sampling, single search term, single day, single country. Coding: two raters - one ophthalmologist and one eye public health physician - independently scored every video, blinded to uploader identity and source category, using DISCERN (16 items: 8 reliability, 7 treatment choice, 1 overall) and PEMAT-A/V (13 understandability, 4 actionability), plus a purpose-built six-domain content score and a misinformation flag benchmarked against International Myopia Institute 2019/2021 reports. Discrepancies resolved by discussion. Reliability reported: ICC 0.957 (0.931-0.972) for DISCERN total; 93.5% agreement and kappa 0.906 for source classification; none reported for the misinformation flag. Statistics: ANOVA/LSD-t or Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni; chi-square or Fisher exact for misleading-prevalence differences.
rob.item6_quote: We also assessed video content quality focusing on misleading information and information coverage about myopia. Content was evaluated using a predefined scoring system based on works published by the International Myopia Institute in 2019 or 2021 (22-25), which were also the standards for characterizing misleading information.
